reviews.review: This is left for dead 3 by another name. It's pretty fun. I see a lot of people saying to wait for a sale, and it's hard to disagree -- BUT it's only slightly overpriced imo.

I bought this game looking for a L4D experience and did not get it. 

Basically go look up decks and builds on line, run the meta, slog your way thru the harder difficults when the rng is in your favor. Cards take time to grind, weapons have set accuracy, mob spawns where ever they want to whenever they want. Its more luck than skill and the little skill it requires is basically doing some homework outside of the game.

I really miss the l4d feel where I could get better at the game, my own accuracy determined how well I could hit tiny targets, and whatever bad luck we encountered our individual mechanics skill could get us through it. 

The only fun I got out of it was playing with friends on the easiest difficulty but that gets way too easy too fast. If it were a cheaper game I'd have said that was enough to recommend.

This game feels like a confusing mash of mechanics that just do not work well together, mixed with many poor / questionable game design decisions.

Add to that the fact that the game's idea of difficulty is simply just to spawn an insane amount of "special" ridden right on top of you.

[h1]Special Ridden[/h1]

The special ridden are, overall, extremely poorly designed. In terms of visuals, sound, and the way that they work, and the way you can counter them. 

To give comparable examples, in Left 4 Dead, each special infected has a very clear silhouette. The Spitter, Charger, Boomer, Jockey, etc, all have very distinguishable visuals. Very easy to identify. On top of that, they play very easily recognizable sounds right before spawning, so that you and the team have time to react to the fact that they are there. And most importantly, they were all designed so that you are able to counter their attacks if you have the skill and reaction to it. 

When the Smoker smokes you, it plays a sound right before attacking, and the tongue takes a while to reach you. During this time, the smoker is very weak so that you can quickly locate and shoot it if you are fast enough. Additionally, you can attack the tongue with a well-timed melee attack as well.  For the hunter and jockey, you can either backtrack and forward-charge with a shove attack to make them stumble temporarily, or even do a well timed shove while they are in the air, right backing attacking you. I can keep on with these examples.

The point is, none of these nuances are to be found in Back 4 Blood. The special ridden seem generally designed to be tanky as hell (able to soak up a whole lot of damage), with attacks that does not in any sense seem designed to have clear counter-mechanics that you can employ. The Tallboy just walks towards you, until it does a last-minute sprint of godlike speed to grab you (if it's the crusher mutation). The spitter variants of the special ridden just have projectiles that fire at the speed of light, making you unable to dodge them, all you can do is try your best to find cover while their insanely low cooldowns means that they just keep on spamming attacks on you. The Retch can spew vomit from 500 km away, also at high velocity. And what they all have in common is that they are basically extremely tanky. In any case, the best "counter" you end up employing is either to run like hell, or simply shoot them as fast as possible, praying that they don't reach you before you do. Now you can try doing this with 5 Tallboys and 4 spitters / hockers, whilst you have a reeker running towards you. I guess because they were too incompetent to come up with better designs, the best way they can increase the difficulty is just to throw all of this at you at once.
I'm not saying the special ridden has to be exactly like what they are in L4D at all. I'm just saying there's no reason why they haven't applied the same wisdom to the design.It clearly works

[h1]Card System[/h1]

The overall idea of the card system is nice, but in practice I think it works poorly with the rest of the game.

The idea of the card system seems to be that you can create decks which represents certain builds. Maybe you make a deck that makes you good with melee, with assault weapons, with shotguns, etc. 

But I don't think that works well with the other RNG elements of the game, and I don't think it plays nicely with balance and corruption cards either. In general, it doesn't play well with the overall dynamic and "adjust as you go along" type of game that B4B tries to be with corruption cards.

First of all, you can make a build that makes you good with a certain type of weapon, sure. But you will not exactly be sure when you will be able to get a good quality weapon of that type because the weapon drops and the store weapons are random. This will matter a whole lot of harder difficulties. Getting what you need for your build to work best will be at the mercy of the RNG gods.

Second of all, decks are very static by nature. You create a deck. You choose one at the start of your run, and then you are locked to that deck for the entirety of that run. No matter what corruption cards are thrown at you, and no matter what else happens in the game. This means that even though the game tries to be dynamic and throw you surprises, you generally can't use your deck to adjust to any of it. Your deck is what it is, and at any one point (after each level), you will only be able to pick 5 cards from your deck, also taking into account that the sequence of cards matters as well. This leaves you very little wiggle room to do any meaningful choice regarding your cards once a run has started.

Honestly, I don't understand why they don't just do away with the concept of decks, and simply allowed people to choose from the entirety of the card pool at the beginning of each level. You will still be able to create builds the same way you do it with decks, the only difference will simply be that players are more free to pick and choose as the game progress. It seems very arbitrary to lock people at a pre-defined stack of 15 cards. What good does that do?

Besides this, balancing with the card system is also a bit... off. When you get to higher difficulties, the powers and abilities of cards matters a [b]lot[/b]. But by the very nature of the design, you will always start out weak. At the start of the run, you will always have fewer cards than at the end. Meaning the game will at times be harder simply by the fact that you don't have access to as many cards as later... it's just odd compared to being equal in power throughout an entire Act / campaign. But maybe that's just me.

[h1]Annoying Design Decisions[/h1]

Then there are the exceedingly annoying smaller design decisions that makes no sense whatsoever, and ruin the overall impression.

First of all, [b]no manual toggle flashlight[/b]. Really? Apparently modern game design loves to take step backs on what seems like obvious, basic functionality. A decade old game like L4D (and many other games) did this. Why can't I toggle my flashlight? Seriously, why? There are many times where I've wanted to toggle the flashlight where the game did not do it for me. And if I have to hear another fanboy tell me to simply "adjust my brightness" I'll go crazy. Why should we have to make either game-wide or system-wide adjustments to make up for such an extremely simply feature that would be so easy to put in, in the first place? Again, it makes no sense.

Second of all, [b]removing attachments cannot be done[/b]. Again, what is this insanity? And yes, I know, they are working on adding a card that does it. But seriously, a [i]card[/i]!? WHY can't it just be something you can do? The only thing this atrocious design decision has done so far is basically punish me and my friends from picking up higher tier weapons because we have had lower tier weapons with better attachments. With all other things that go on in the game of RNG, why should it be a risk to pick up another weapon and just pray to the RNG gods that you then get the attachments you want later? I just don't understand it.

Third of all, car alarms and door alarms are designed extremely poorly in relation to projectiles. You can trigger cars and doors miles and miles ahead in the level that you have no chance of currently seeing, because there seemingly are no radius at which the player has to be within before shooting alarms triggers them. This doesn't provide any good. No amount of skill will be able to get you out of that situation, besides constantly shooting towards the ground. Maybe you think that's good design, I certainly don't. You're punishing the player for something he/she is not yet able to react to.

There are many other points I could make... but these were the ones that just seem to stick out the most...

All in all, not really recommended. Go play something like L4D instead :)

From playing, I can say the game is fun, but it has a lot of issues although they arent the hardest thing in the world to fix.

There are 2 big problems that I personally have with this game.

1: Special infected feel more like DPS checks than actual special infected with counterplay.
Take Left 4 Dead as a good example of how specials work, there is a musical warning when they spawn, they always make distinct audio when attacking, and look far different from other infected.
They aren't too spongy either, so its completely up to the players skill in determining where and when an attack is coming from and acting accordingly.
But in Back 4 Blood, basically all Special infected feel more like a DPS check than anything else, there is no warning when they spawn, and most of them don't really have counterplay other than tank some damage and hope they die before you do and that's especially true with this games version of a spitter.
Its also good to note that there are a few infected that look borderline the same but do completely different things especially to new players, with these being the 2 tallboy variants

That also goes nicely into the second problem
2: A lot of damage in this game is completely unavoidable.
With the few examples i will use the Hockers and the Retches.

First of all, there is zero reason the Hockers projectile should deal damage over time, because A: its nearly impossible to dodge 53 fast moving spitballs, and B: It requires a teammate to not shoot the webbing, but go into the line of fire of other infected to MELEE you. (Because that makes sense)
Next up with the Retches, well its just a worse version of the Hocker since there is actually no way to dodge it.
You can run out of the way, you can jump out of the way, you can go behind a wall but it will ALWAYS hit you and is completely unavoidable.
And this issue is also exaggerated by the fact that they are all super spongy.
Now look, i don't mind BOSS enemies being spongy, but the specials should not feel literally just like DPS checks, thats not really fun, and im not even going to bother mentioning the $60 price tag because we all know the problem with that.

As much as i would love to say "Yes go buy it its super fun" because i honestly still enjoy the game with its pretty in depth deck building and whatnot, until these issues are fixed i cant say its worth $60, until then its a No.
(Also please let us remove attachments without having to find a worse or alternate one that makes zero sense
 thank you)

Edit: Fixed some typos.

As it stands, I'd give this game a D. Playing with friends, in voice chat, after unlocking a lot of cards and coordinating your decks, and the AI Director isn't doing his best to make sure you aren't having fun, it can feel like a C.
It's almost Left 4 Dead 3 but... falls short.
To be clear, I bought the Ultimate Edition. I don't regret it. I'm gonna keep playing it, but I haven't recommended it to anybody, and have talked a couple friends into at least waiting for a sale.

The game is either going too easy, or it's too punishing. 
The AI Director either leaves you alone, or gives you 5 of each special infected at once. 
Recruit is too easy, Veteran spikes the difficulty way too hard, and Nightmare is simply masochistic.
The grind doesn't feel worth it. The cosmetics are uninteresting. 
Unlocking the cards was... tedious. I'd get it if I felt like I was picking up skills along the way, but strategy seems totally out the window. It's a frenzied mess. Zombies spawn from everywhere. I wish it felt more like clearing areas out, but... they just spawn in from wherever. 
The deck building is almost good. 
Some of the cards are poorly worded - vague, confusing. Some cards don't seem to trigger, or have conditions that almost never happen.
A LOT of cards have downsides to them, and they often feel disproportionate to the bonus you get.
A lot of cards have the same downside, so you cumulatively end up with a huge penalty like -60% stamina or -30% damage resistance
How come the mutation cards don't have downsides? We have a card that gives us +25% damage but -30% health; the mutations just get +50% damage, +50% health, also heals when it does damage to you, also is armored, also does 100% trauma damage instead of regular damage, and, like fighting a hydra, you kill 1 and 2 more are coming around the corner.
I have lots of complaints. I could keep going, honestly. 

I will say a couple nice things.
This game has some of the best-looking fog I have ever seen in a video game, ever.
I like the safe room notes, and the stuffed turtles. And looking for the secret golden skulls. I'm still looking for a couple!
Some sections are pretty good. 
Like I said, I'm gonna keep playing it. I'm just not going to recommend it.

It's more of a roguelite/deckbuilder than just a horde shooter. Worth checking out.

If you're looking for a Left 4 Dead successor, look no further. This is literally it. They've also added a card system, which I havent fully dived into yet, since I love just going around killing Zombies. You have to make sure to explore a lot, as there's money and items all over the place. I've got to say as a Left 4 Dead fan, I am extremely satisfied in this intriguing sequel. It is very replayable, a friend of mine has replayed the campaign from beginning to end several times now.

As a fan of the L4D series I had high hopes for B4B hence why this review is a kinda mixed bag.

Although this game differs in some few ways it seems to lack the finesse of its older counter parts. 
Firstly having paid a considerable amount for even the basic game download I feel obligated to play to justify the spend...then unfortunately it soon becomes apparent that the lack of content does not warrant the price tag.  The maps throughout the campaigns first run are somewhat impressive only then to discover that several are just repeats with a different route.
Now don't get me wrong, the game has its moments of fun regardless of repetitiveness however, the lack of a decent block\guard leaves you helpless to various attacks that really start to irritate you.

Workshop content and mapping tools is an absolute must in order for this game to have any chance of surviving and not turning into a complete worm face.  

NOW If any of the devs are reading this.....refund the additional cost to players that purchased anything above the basic pack, remove the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing from xbox game pass (yeah that's right, players are able to play via gamepass for 3 months at a whopping £1 price tag) open community tools up for modders and then watch game sales soar.

The game is terrific, and I had zero (0) interest in playing it when they first announced it. But the devs did the impossible and made an enjoyable, online, cooperative shooter with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cards/deck building being the main progression system. If you're a nostalgia baby trapped in 2009, stick with L4D and pretend you're 12 years younger and happier again. If you want something new and unique, suck this game down like the dirty ♥♥♥♥♥ you are.

Back 4 Blood:
~~~~~~~~~~ 

Humankind is on the verge of extinction due to a deadly parasite that mutates humans into dangerous creatures. They have been named the Ridden by a small group of survivors who have the tiny task of finding a way to destroy them and save humanity. While most of the Ridden look like normal human beings (slightly decomposed), others have mutated several times into giant and powerful beasts. They all have one thing in common . . . if they see you, they will come at you like flies to a fresh cow pat, and it will not be pretty! So, are you ready to face the Ridden onslaught? Because it’s going to be tough, gruesome and full of Zombies in Back 4 Blood!

Back 4 Blood is a first-person Zombie action game developed by Turtle Rocks Studios and published by Warner Bros. Games on the 13th of October 2021 on the Steam platform. The game is also available on PS4, PS5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X|S and Microsoft Windows.

The game consists of two modes of play, which are the Campaign and the Swarm modes. The Campaign mode can be played solo or online via an individual platform such as PC, Xbox or PlayStation, and can also be set as Crossplay if you don’t mind playing with people who use another platform. My review is mainly based on a solo campaign and several online co-op games on PC and Crossplay. 

After launching the game and signing in, you’ll arrive at the Survivor’s Camp. There, you’ll be able to try every single weapon in the shooting range, and go to the armoury to see the skins you have (or will unlock) for each of the weapons. Two tables, one where you can create your next deck of cards and the other where you can purchase new cards. You’ll also have two tents, one where you can customise your character and the other where you can set or continue a run (game).

In terms of difficulty, there are three: Recruit, Veteran and Nightmare. I find the Recruit difficulty extremely easy, while Veteran is more like hardcore, and Nightmare is truly difficult. Interestingly, in my few Crossplay games with Xbox gamers, everyone (console gamers) was amazed at the difficulty when they joined my game set on the Veteran difficulty. 

I didn’t like playing Back 4 Blood in Crossplay at all, as it was laggy most of the time and probably too difficult for console gamers on the level of difficulty I set! I didn’t enjoy playing with other PC gamers either, as it was clear to me that these players knew most of the levels and were more interested in speed running each level rather than keeping up with a newcomer, and this is probably one of the negative points of the game. Not only does it take at least 10 minutes to find an online game, but when you find one, you’ll be playing with people who have more experience than you.  On the flip side, it would be extremely fun to play this game with your mates!

So, playing a solo campaign was actually much better than playing with other people online. There are some issues here, too, such as the bots AI is dumb, to say the least. One or two bots might get stuck in an area for a while, or when you are down, and while waiting to be healed back, the bot stays in front of you doing nothing and therefore you and your party fail to reach the saferoom because you all die.

However, I did enjoy the game for many reasons. The first one is that you have a total of 32 missions divided into 4 Acts. As I write this review, I am currently playing the third act, and I am having a lot of fun. So far, a larger number of the missions have been long, while a few were quite short but intense in terms of fighting. I also like that you receive an additional difficulty or rewards from the corruption cards at the start of each mission. For example, you might have 5 corruption cards at the start of each mission, but only one will be chosen as you start the run. To give you an idea, if you were to play the entire act 1, which has 13 missions, it would mean that 13 corruption cards would be added to your run and it would become really difficult, especially on the Veteran and Nightmare difficulties. You’ll also have active cards which are relevant to your deck card (s). So, as you start the next mission, you’ll be given a few cards to choose from, which will hopefully help you through whatever follows.

After choosing 1 of 4 characters available to you at first, there are another 4 characters to unlock. Right from the start, you’ll be thrown into the thick of it. You’ll start the run in the safehouse. There, you’ll be able to purchase all sorts of items, from weapons to extra inventory slots for you and your party. When you are ready to rock and roll, you just have to open the safehouse door to face the music. 

As soon as Ridden sees your group, they will start coming at you super-fast. You’ll need to be very careful not to activate car alarms and security doors, or to scare the birds, as it will make noise and therefore attract another wave of Ridden.  The next wave of Ridden is usually more aggressive and will also have bigger Ridden, such as the tallboy, which has a huge, strong arm and can do heavy damage to your health if you are on the receiving end of it.  There are a few other big and powerful Ridden in this game, and I particularly like the mini-boss that runs after you and tries to gobble down its oesophagus. It’s inevitable that you’ll find yourself down on many occasions, but hopefully one of the other players or bots will heal you before you die.  But let’s suppose that you do die while playing on the solo campaign; in that case, you’ll automatically become one of the other three characters until you free your initial character ,who will be trapped in a sort of cocoon somewhere further down the track. Then you are able to play again with the character you had chosen before starting the run.  

As you go through each mission, you’ll find cases on the floor that hold many essential goodies such as bandages, health kits, weapons, weapons attachments and ammunition. You’ll also have a mini-gun case, but you’ll need a tool kit to open it. The other collectable you’ll find around is money which you need in order to purchase additional items in the safehouse. Intel are cards, of which some are free, and others will cost money to activate into your current run. It is a lot of fun.
